ut_reservoir_wall.blurb: Reservoir Wall is a trad crack cliff in Indian Creek canyon, cut into the canyon's red sandstone. Nearly every line here is a crack, with a couple of top-rope options mixed in. Difficulty runs from the high 5.9s up into the low 5.13s, but the bulk of the climbs sit between 5.10 and 5.12, so it suits parties already comfortable on Creek-style jamming. The wall holds shade for much of the day, which makes it a good pick when other Creek walls are baking. Be aware that part of the cliff, the section that faces the road, is on private ground, so stick to the established climbs. Sandstone here is fragile after rain, and facilities are minimal.
ut_reservoir_wall.parking_note: Drive roughly 8 miles along UT-211 beyond Newspaper Rock, with the reservoir passing on your right. A small pullout sits on the right, directly across the road from the Beef Basin turnoff.

ut_supercrack_buttress.blurb: Supercrack Buttress stands at the mouth of Donnelly Canyon in Indian Creek and is among the busiest walls in the whole canyon. The rock is Wingate sandstone split by clean cracks, flakes and slots, nearly all of it trad, with a single top-rope and one boulder problem thrown in. Most of the climbs fall in the 5.10 to 5.11 range, with a scattering of easier lines below and a few 5.12 and 5.13 testpieces above. Protection is good and the walk from the road is short and well beaten, so it makes a fine first stop for learning crack technique. Expect company on any pleasant weekend, and bring a plan for waste since toilets are scarce. Wet sandstone is fragile, so skip it after rain.
ut_supercrack_buttress.parking_note: The dirt lot at the Donnelly Canyon trailhead serves the wall, about 4 miles past Newspaper Rock along UT-211. A worn path leads from the lot to the base.

ut_pistol_whipped.blurb: Pistol Whipped is a west-facing sandstone buttress in Indian Creek, devoted almost entirely to trad crack climbing. The wall picks up good afternoon sun, so it works on a cold day and can be timed for shade in the heat. Climbing here leans hard: most lines are 5.10 and 5.11, a healthy handful reach 5.12, and a few go beyond, with very little at easier grades. Because plaques are scarce, a topo or a friend who knows the wall helps a lot. The drive in uses dirt tracks that cross a creek, so check conditions first, and the final approach follows a cairned path up a shallow wash and over talus. Wet sandstone is easily damaged, so wait out any rain.
ut_pistol_whipped.parking_note: Reached by dirt roads running south from the junction of UT-211 and the Beef Basin road, including a creek crossing a decent 2WD car can often manage. Pull off the road right beneath the point of the buttress.
ut_pistol_whipped.approach: From the pullout, follow a cairned trail up a shallow wash, then climb talus to the base of the wall.

ut_prophesy_wall.blurb: Prophesy Wall is a sandstone cliff of roughly 200 to 250 feet in the desert north of St. George, known for long bolted face routes that go in two or three pitches. Holds include side pulls, underclings and small bulges. Much of the climbing is 5.9 and 5.10, with some easier routes and a few harder ones, and a single 60 m rope handles most descents. Opening pitches often climb easier than their grades suggest. The wall catches afternoon sun in winter and sits in shade in the morning, and summer is very hot. Sandstone breaks when wet, so give it a day or two after rain. Bring water and pack out waste, and note that gunfire can be heard nearby.
ut_prophesy_wall.parking_note: Take Bluff Street north from St. George, turn off onto gravel near the 18-mile marker, and follow the roads past Sand Cove Reservoir to a dirt track below the wall. Leave the car near the big iron pipe where the trail begins.

ut_2nd_meat_wall.blurb: 2nd Meat Wall is a trad crack cliff in Indian Creek, popular for its shade on warm days. Nearly every route is a sandstone crack, with an occasional top-rope option and at least one two-pitch line. The climbing is stout: almost all of it falls between 5.10 and 5.12, with a handful at 5.13 and only a rare easier pitch. A decent trail climbs from the parking area to the base. The access road is poor, so a low car should go carefully, and Original Meat Wall lies farther along an even rougher road. Wet sandstone is easily damaged, so wait after rain. Toilets are limited, so carry out your waste.
ut_2nd_meat_wall.parking_note: Turn off the highway west of Cat Wall onto a gated dirt road, rough in places. A parking area at its end serves this wall.

ut_south_west_end_pink_lady_area.blurb: This is the southwestern edge of the boulder fields in Moe's Valley outside St. George, home to Pink Lady and a run of popular problems on grainy orange-brown sandstone. Expect a mix of slopers, crimps and cracks that is rough on skin. Problems range from easy to very hard, but the largest share sits between V2 and V6, so moderate boulderers will find plenty to work. Mornings tend to offer the best shade, and winter is the popular time to visit. From the end of the road, the farthest boulders are within about a quarter hour on foot. The rock is soft, so treat it gently.
ut_south_west_end_pink_lady_area.parking_note: Use the marked climbing lot at the end of the valley road. Higher clearance is helpful on the final stretch.
ut_south_west_end_pink_lady_area.approach: Continue past the Teepee Boulder heading south, keeping to the right.

ut_south_end.blurb: South End is the southern section of the Moe's Valley boulders near St. George, Utah. The stone is grainy orange-brown sandstone with slopers, crimps and cracks, and it is tough on fingertips. Difficulty is wide: from a few very easy problems up through V12, with the heaviest concentration between V2 and V6. Because the rock is soft, avoid climbing it when damp and brush holds gently. Fall through spring is the comfortable season; summer heat is a poor fit.
ut_south_end.parking_note: Park in the marked climbing lot at the end of the valley road, then walk in to the boulders. Higher clearance helps on the last stretch.
